title: Conservative (Masorti) Judaism
hook: halakha as binding, and developing through history

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: new roles. Women as scholars and advisers in Orthodox settings, and a debate inside the law about how far those roles reach. Did you read how one role is described? Today, a movement that answers the question of change differently. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

Every seventh year, the Torah says, debts are released. A generous law. But the Mishnah tells what happened next: as the seventh year drew near, people stopped lending to the poor, afraid they would never be repaid. The Torah had warned against exactly that, the thought in the heart that says the year of release is at hand. So Hillel, the great sage, enacted the prozbul, a court document that kept loans collectible, so that lending would go on. The goal of the law was kept by changing how it worked. Hold onto that story. Today's movement points to it.
screen: `DEBTS RELEASED IN THE SEVENTH YEAR.` → `PEOPLE STOP LENDING.` → `HILLEL'S PROZBUL.`

segments.voice: Masorti. It is the Hebrew word for traditional, from masoret, tradition. In North America the movement is called Conservative Judaism; in Israel and elsewhere, Masorti. Turn it four ways. First, halakha is binding. Conservative Judaism holds that Jewish law obligates Jews: Shabbat, kashrut, prayer, the festivals. That sets it apart from movements that see the law as guidance only. Second, the law has a history. Conservative scholars study how halakha grew: the Bible, the Mishnah, the Talmud, the codes, each generation adding and adjusting. They point to moments like Hillel's prozbul, where sages changed how a law worked in order to keep its purpose. Third, so the law can still develop. If it developed before, the movement holds, it may develop now, carefully, by rabbis trained in the sources, reasoning from inside the tradition, with history in view. Orthodox Judaism also answers new questions from inside the law, as we heard; the difference is in how far change may go, and who may make it. Fourth, the deep root. The tractate of the Fathers opens: Moses received the Torah and handed it on, masar, to Joshua. Masoret, tradition, is something handed on. Deuteronomy says: "ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee." The movement hears in that a tradition that is both received and alive, passing through human hands, and shaped by them. Tomorrow, how those hands actually make decisions.
screen: `MASORTI MEANS TRADITIONAL.` · `HALAKHA IS BINDING.` · `THE LAW HAS A HISTORY.` · `SO IT CAN STILL DEVELOP.` · then, large: `ASK THY FATHER, AND HE WILL SHEW THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep the purpose. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one habit or rule you started for a good reason: a budget, a morning routine, a house rule about phones at dinner. Ask what it was for. Is it still doing that, or, like the year of release, has it started working against its own aim? If it has, picture one small change that would serve the purpose better, the way Hillel's court document kept lending alive. You don't have to make the change. Just see it. Then let it rest, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Masorti. Traditional: the name for Conservative Judaism in Israel and elsewhere, which holds halakha as binding and as developing through history. Today's word.
Your line: tradition and change. Today, learn one Conservative ruling, any one, and ask what purpose of the law it was trying to keep. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-one.

notes: 'Masorti is the Hebrew word for traditional, from masoret, tradition' and its link to masar in Avot 1:1 is a word-root claim; confirm it is acceptable (standard Hebrew).
'In North America the movement is called Conservative Judaism; in Israel and elsewhere, Masorti. is unsourced; confirm.
Mishnah Shevi'it 10:3 (Hillel saw people refraining from lending and enacted the prozbul) and Deuteronomy 15:9 (the warning) are paraphrased.
The contrast with Orthodoxy is framed as a difference in how far change may go and who may make it, without ranking; confirm fairness to both.
The positive-historical school (Zecharias Frankel) and the movement's founding history are deliberately not named or dated.
